========================================================
Empirical Research Plan:  “Transit Expansion → Property Values”
========================================================

--------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------
Preferred approach: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with an event-study
panel specification at the property (or 100 × 100 m grid-cell) level.

Why appropriate?  
• The transit line is introduced on a known date, after a long pre-period.  
• Only properties “close” to the new stations receive the treatment; farther
properties serve as natural controls.  
• Property transactions are observed repeatedly through time, so we can compare
the evolution of prices for treated vs. control areas before and after opening,
testing the parallel-trends assumption via an event study.  
• Station openings may be staggered along the line (different stops open at
different times), so we implement the recent “sun-abadi / Callaway-Sant’Anna /
Borusyak–Jaravel” estimators to avoid heterogeneous-treatment-timing bias.

--------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition
--------------------------------------------------------
• Treatment indicator: Treat_i = 1 if the centroid of property i lies within
800 meters (≈½ mile, standard “walkable” buffer) of any new station; 0 otherwise.

• Control group: Properties located 1,500–3,000 meters from any new station,
outside the likely walking catchment but still in the same housing market
(maximises similarity while minimising direct impact).  We drop observations
within 800–1,500 m to create a clean gap (“donut”) and mitigate spillovers.

• Treatment timing:  
   – t = T₀ + k, where T₀ is the opening month of the closest station for each
treated property.  If stations open on different dates, each property receives
its own exposure date.  

   – We also code two anticipation periods: Announcement (public release of the
final route) and Construction start.  These show up as leads in the event study.

• If one preferred a geographic RDD, the running variable would be distance to
the nearest new station with a cutoff at 800 m, but we treat that as a
robustness check, not the primary design.

--------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: Absent the transit line, average log-price trends for
treated and control properties would have been identical.  Plausibility:
Same metropolitan housing cycle, controls chosen from nearby neighbourhoods,
pre-trend testable in the event study.

A2. No Differential Shocks: No other policy or amenity changed at exactly the
same time and only in treated areas.  Plausibility strengthened by adding tract
× year FE and controlling for new retail permits, school openings, etc.

A3. Stable Composition (SUTVA & no sorting): The set of sold properties and
buyers is not endogenously selected by treatment in a way that biases repeat-
sales prices.  We will include property fixed effects (repeat-sales) and test
for changes in observable characteristics.

A4. Spillovers limited to donut exclusion zone: Impacts beyond 1,500 m are
negligible; otherwise control prices might be treated indirectly.  Sensitivity
to bandwidths will be shown.

--------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------
T1. Non-parallel pre-trends (gentrification already underway near stations).  
   • Mitigation: Visual and statistical test of pre-period leads; include tract-
     specific linear time trends; use repeat-sales estimator; propensity score
     re-weighting to equalise observables.

T2. Anticipatory capitalisation (prices rise at route announcement, not opening).  
   • Mitigation: Event-study specification with announcement and construction
     leads; define alternative treatment dates (announcement vs. opening) and
     estimate each; bound the effect.

T3. Simultaneous neighbourhood improvements orchestrated with transit (e.g.,
streetscaping, zoning up-rezoning).  
   • Mitigation: Control for building permits, FAR changes, and commercial
     vacancy rates at census-block × year level; exclude stations accompanied by
     bespoke TOD rezoning in a robustness sample.

--------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------
```r
#-------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#-------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(sf)             # spatial operations
library(fixest)         # high-dimensional FE DiD
library(did)            # Callaway-Sant’Anna estimator
library(ggplot2)

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and merge data
#-------------------------------------------------------
trans <- fread("property_transactions.csv")   # full sample
stations <- st_read("new_stations.geojson")   # point shapefile
trans_sf <- st_as_sf(trans, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
trans_sf <- st_transform(trans_sf, crs = st_crs(stations))

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct distance & treatment variables
#-------------------------------------------------------
trans_sf$dist_station <- st_distance(trans_sf, stations) |> 
                         apply(1, min) |> as.numeric()

# treatment buffer
treated_radius  <- 800      # in metres
control_in      <- 1500
control_out     <- 3000

trans_sf[, treat := (dist_station <= treated_radius)]
trans_sf[, control := (dist_station >= control_in & 
                       dist_station <= control_out)]

# keep treated + control
sample <- trans_sf[treat | control]

# Treatment timing: nearest station opening date
nearest_station_id <- st_nearest_feature(sample, stations)
sample$open_date   <- stations$open_date[nearest_station_id]

# Event time
sample$date        <- as.Date(sample$sale_date)
sample$event_time  <- as.numeric(round((sample$date - sample$open_date)/30.44)) # months

# leads/lags for event-study (e.g., −36 to +60 months)
sample[, event_grp := fifelse(event_time < -36, -36,
                       fifelse(event_time > 60,  60, event_time))]

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DiD regression (two-way FE)
#-------------------------------------------------------
feols(log(price) ~ i(event_grp, treat, ref = -1) + 
                     property_fe + month_fe | 0,
      data = sample,
      cluster = "tract_id") -> est_event

iplot(est_event)      # plot dynamic effects

# Simplified DiD average effect post-opening (k ≥ 0)
sample[, post := (event_time >= 0)]
feols(log(price) ~ treat*post + property_fe + month_fe,
      data = sample,
      cluster = "tract_id") -> est_avg

#-------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: Donut bandwidth 500m / 1000m
#-------------------------------------------------------
bandwidth_test <- function(rad){
  smp <- trans_sf[(dist_station <= rad) | 
                  (dist_station >= rad*1.75 & dist_station <= rad*3)]
  smp[, treat := (dist_station <= rad)]
  smp[, post  := (as.Date(sale_date) >= open_date)]
  feols(log(price) ~ treat*post + property_fe + month_fe,
        data = smp, cluster = "tract_id")
}

est_500 <- bandwidth_test(500)
est_1000 <- bandwidth_test(1000)
etable(list(est_avg, est_500, est_1000),
       tex = FALSE, se.below = TRUE)
```

--------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts positive capitalization: improved accessibility raises housing
demand near stations, shifting the bid-rent curve upward.  Prior U.S. light-rail
studies often find 4 – 8 percent higher prices within ½ mile.  Given line
characteristics (frequency, CBD connectivity), I expect a 5–7 percent increase
in log sale price for treated properties post-opening, with slightly smaller
effects if anticipation already priced in.

--------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
--------------------------------------------------------
C1: Clear treatment definition and timing ……………………………… 1  
C2: Parallel pre-trends supported by data (will test) …………… 0.8  
C3: No time-varying composition or selection bias ………………… 0.7  
C4: No concurrent shocks differentially hitting groups ………… 0.6  
C5: Correct inference (clustering, staggered timing estimator) 1  

Overall average ≈ 0.82 → reasonably credible but still reliant on
parallel-trend diagnostics and spillover tests.

========================================================
